name: SQLite (small-blob read/write vs filesystem, kvtest)
baseline: Filesystem storage of one file per blob (stdio fopen/fread/fwrite or open/read/write/close per blob)
metric: throughput (blob read and write time) and disk space
workload: kvtest (test/kvtest.c in the SQLite tree): read and write of roughly 10 KB blobs (100K blobs with sizes uniformly distributed between 8K and 12K, about 1 GB total) from one SQLite database versus the same blobs as individual files on disk, measured June 2017 with a SQLite version between 3.19.2 and 3.20.0.
claimed_speedup: SQLite reads and writes small blobs about 35% faster than fread()/fwrite() on individual files (page title: '35% Faster Than The Filesystem'); a database of 10 KB blobs also uses about 20% less disk space than the pile of files.
compiler_and_flags: Build recipe in the kvtest.c header comment: gcc -Os -I. -DSQLITE_THREADSAFE=0 -DSQLITE_OMIT_LOAD_EXTENSION kvtest.c sqlite3.c on Linux/Mac, cl -I. kvtest.c sqlite3.c on Windows with MSVC; the exact flags behind the published 2017 numbers were not confirmed.
stars_or_usage: 10.6k stars on the official GitHub mirror; embedded in nearly every OS, browser and phone
tradeoffs: Claim covers small blobs of about 10 KB only; SQLite adds a SQL engine, locking and a single-file database, so it is not a drop-in for large files. Public domain dedication with no patent grant.
caveats: Evidence tier is capped at C because sqlite.org was unreachable from this environment (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND in WebFetch, proxy CONNECT 403 for curl) and so were the mirrors tried (www2.sqlite.org, gwern.net, docs.w3cub.com, underpop.online.fr, shapeof.com); the 35% and 20% figures, the blob sizes and the June 2017 date come from WebSearch result summaries of the page, not from the page itself. CPU models per machine and the exact flags behind the numbers were not seen (summary says all test machines used SSD except one Windows 7 hard-drive machine); the benchmark program kvtest.c is public (opened via github.com/sqlite/sqlite test/kvtest.c) so the result is reproducible and a retier to A or B is plausible once the page is reachable. The page calls 35% approximate and says results vary with hardware and OS, and that some reviewers saw higher latency than direct I/O; a Lobsters commenter argued filesystem prefetching explains part of the gap, and a reader reported 47% on a Mac HFS system. The page is first-party (SQLite authors) and measures 2017 code. Other search summaries mention a Windows 10 read gain of about 5x and an Android gain of about 35% in another page version; those were not verified. Separate and obsolete: sqlite.org/speed.html (SQLite 2.7.6 vs PostgreSQL 7.1.3 and MySQL 3.23.41, 2001) says SQLite was often 10-20x faster than default PostgreSQL on common operations but the page itself calls its numbers meaningless today; not used as the claim. The suggested baselines SQLite and PostgreSQL do not apply to this claim since SQLite is the incumbent for embedded SQL storage.
found_via: seed-list mining backfill: awesome-cpp#Database and awesome-c#Database listing for SQLite; WebSearch 'SQLite "35% faster than the filesystem"' summaries; github.com/sqlite/sqlite and test/kvtest.c opened
